# LED Bracelet

## Overview

Sew a circuit\! This project includes the design and construction of a wearable LED bracelet. The bracelet is in a layer textile “sandwich” structure to safely embed a circuit in the e-textile. The engineering goals of the project are electrical insulation, user comfort, easy maintainability, and gain experience with conductive thread.

The bracelet structure: a cotton top layer,  felt middle layer containing the sewn LED circuit, and a cotton bottom layer. Felt is used as the circuit’s substrate because it is a natural insulator, prevents conductive thread from shifting, and provides stability while still allowing the circuit to bend. The outer cotton layers provide protection to the circuit from friction, moisture, and contact to skin, creating safety and comfort for wearing.

To support easy maintenance, the bracelet sewn shut on three sides, leaving a short side left open to create a pocket. This pocket allows the circuit layer to be inserted/removed for battery change or switching the circuit on and off. A button closure near the pocket connects the bracelet to the user’s wrist and closes the fourth side, preventing the circuit layer from sliding out while being worn. 

This document covers the construction process and design considerations for the bracelet and circuit.

## Components

Circuit  
Sewable battery holder (LilyPad)  
Lilypad LEDs (x3)  
Conductive thread (stainless steel)  
Felt  
Multimeter  
CR2032 battery (3V)  
Jumper wires  
Clear non-gel nail polish  
Sewing pins

Bracelet   
Cotton fabric (x2) (3 in x 8.75in)  
Button  
Sewing machine and sewing accessories  
Needle 

General  
Sewing pins  
Scissors 

## Process

1. ## Experiment with the battery holder, a battery, and a LED. 

For testing I used jumper wires to connect the battery holder to an LED. The battery holder has an on and off switch on it. Testing that the components work.   
![][image3]

2. ## Experiment with LEDs in parallel

I was testing how many LEDs could be connected in parallel while all are still very bright

- I found that 3 LEDs could be powered and still be very bright  
- In the image below I hand sewed the battery pack to Felt material. (Felt is good insulator) I sewed the positive terminals together and the negative terminals together, to ensure the battery pack was stable and not going to shift around during testing.

![][image4]

3. ## Which LEDS

I decided to use a yellow cotton fabric for the top layer of the bracelet and a dark blue cotton fabric for the bottom layer. The thinking is that yellow is a lighter color and will allow more of the emitted light of the LEDs to pass through. While the dark blue will block emitted light from going through the side that will be touching the arm.

- I had a pack of LilyPad LEDs: Pink, Red, White, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange  
- I wanted to use 3 different colors  
- I found the Yellow, Red, and Green LED had a ‘bright intensity’ of emitted light shown, didn’t drown each other out while covered by the yellow fabric, and I liked the combination  
-  (Reminded me of a stop light)

![][image5]  
These were different testing interactions of deciding what LEDs to use. The LEDs are in the same set up as the previous step with sewing pins keeping the positions of the LEDs while testing.  
![][image6]

4. ## Position of LEDS

I wanted the battery pack and LEDs to be placed where the arm is ‘roughly’ flat to limit poor connections with the thread and fabric bending. The path of the circuit is a battery pack and 3 LEDs in parallel. I was also aware that the threaded path of the conductive thread should be short because the longer the thread is, the more resistance the thread adds to the circuit. I cut the felt to be long enough to cover my wrist while testing positions of the LEDs. Used sewing pins to test the position of the LEDs and keep the felt around my wrist  
![][image7]  
![][image8]

5. ## Sewing a Circuit

I used conductive thread made of stainless steel as the thread and the wires between the electrical components. I hand sewed the components. Sewing a path of positive battery terminals to all of the positive terminals of the LEDs and did the same for the negative terminals.

- I did an LED at a time. So \+ and \- of the green.  Tested that the battery could turn on the LED, repeat with the yellow and red LEDs

- I used a running stitch between the components 

- At a terminal pad, I made 3+ loops to secure the connection. 

- If the thread was not long enough to make to the next component and make the loops, I tied it off and started the new thread with making some more  loops at the current LED to be able to pass the signal to the next part

- Note: Power should be OFF while sewing the circuit

- Note: the thread needs to be tight\! If there is slack in the thread that could cause issues with signal

- Note: It’s important to cut the leads short on the knots to prevent short circuits.

- Improvement: I should have tested more on how the LEDs reacted to bending the fabric to test the quality of the connections, by seeing if the LEDs flickered

![][image9]![][image10]![][image11]

6. ## Insulation by Nail Polish

Conductive Thread is basically a wire that is not insulated. To prevent fraying of the thread and breaking the electrical connection I coat the thread with clear non-gel nail polish with three layers. 

- I tested that the circuit had no issues after the first and three coats

7. ## Sewing the Bracelet

At first I sewed the bottom bracelet. However it was too small to easily put the circuit inside of it. So I cut the length and width of the felt, that helped. Then when the circuit was inside of the sleeve, the seam allowance blocked some of the emitted light.(seam allowance is the fabric that is between the end of the fabric and the stitching.  
I decided to resew the bracelet to be bigger (3in x 8.75 in).The seam allowance was no longer in the way of the emitted light, easier to place the circuit inside of it, and the LED were no longer tightly pressed against the yellow fabric when it was around my wrist.

- Straight stitch with Sewing Machine with the right sides of the fabrics touching along 3 sides leaving a soft side open  
- Flip the material inside out so that the right side of the fabric is on the outside and the seams are on the inside  
- On the open side, fold inward enough fabric to make a hem and sew it with the sewing machine. (This prevents loose strands from being in the away of the felt’s movement in and out of the opening  
- Mark with a writing utensil where the button hole and closure should be  
- Sewing Machine’s button hole settings to form the button hole enclosure   
- Seam ripper to make the button hole in the enclosure for it.  
- Hand sew the button on

I used the sewing machine for connecting the fabrics together,creating the button hole, and at the edge of the opening side. I hand sewed the button on. I folded over the edge of fabric at the opening and sewed them down to remove loose cotton thread that was getting in the way of the movement of the circuit.  
![][image12]

The circuit in the original bracelet.  
![][image13]

The circuit in the final bracelet.  
![][image14]  
Final Product:  
	The final bracelet was comfortable. It was easy to access the circuit through the opening when the bracelet was unbuttoned. When the circuit is in the bracelet is protected. Occasionally the red LED will flicker, tapping the red LED usually fixes the issue. A great introduction to wearable electronics.

Goal: Introduction to e-textiles. A bracelet with a LED circuit inside. This is my first time sewing a circuit or using components from LilyPad. I have done more hand-sewing than  machine sewing; I would like to improve my ability to use a sewing machine.

When checked with the multimeter the battery voltage: 2.8V and the LEDs when lighted was 2.3V   
![][image15]![][image16]![][image17]![][image18]  
	

## In the process… I Learned…

- How to replace a needle on a sewing machine  
- Get the sewing machine’s needle unstuck from going to far near the bobbin  
- How to sew a button hole with the sewing machine   
- Experience with conductive thread and problem solving with it for insulation and ensuring an electronic connection  
- Before cutting the conductive thread do more testing of bending the felt while the circuit is on to be sure the connection is stable. (test for flickering)
